opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a really important question, and I think it's one where people's intuitions can be pulled in quite different directions.

The basic idea is that once AI systems become capable enough to meaningfully contribute to AI research itself, you could get a feedback loop. Research that would have taken human teams five years might get done in one, because you have many copies of capable systems working in parallel, around the clock, and potentially faster than humans can think. So it's not crazy. There's a coherent mechanism there.

But I'd want to separate a few things. First, there's the question of what's actually driving progress. Over the last decade, a lot of the gains have come not from clever algorithmic insights but from scaling up compute: bigger training runs, more data, more hardware. If that's the dominant input, then automating the researchers doesn't automatically speed things up fivefold. You'd still be bottlenecked on chip fabrication, on power, on building data centres, on physical things that don't move at the speed of software. You can't think your way to a new fab.

Second, even on the algorithmic side, research involves running experiments, and experiments take compute. So if you have a million brilliant automated researchers but the same number of GPUs, they're all queuing for the same resources. You might get better ideas about which experiments to run, which is valuable, but it's not the same as a clean multiplication of progress.

That said, I don't want to be dismissive. I think the probability of something like this happening is high enough that it deserves serious attention, and what worries me most isn't really the exact speed-up factor. It's what it does to our ability to respond. Much of our safety strategy, our governance, and our capacity to notice problems and course-correct relies on there being time: time for evidence to accumulate, for institutions to deliberate, for norms to form. If five years of progress happens in one year, then a lot of those mechanisms, which already struggle to keep pace, could simply be outrun. Regulators who expected to have a few years to respond to a capability might find it's already been surpassed.

So my overall view would be something like this: I'm uncertain about whether we'd get that kind of compression, and I think there are real physical and practical bottlenecks that make the most dramatic versions less likely than some people suggest. But the consequences if it does happen are severe enough, and the warning time potentially short enough, that we should be preparing for it now: building the monitoring, the institutional capacity, and the agreements that would let us slow down or pause if we saw that kind of acceleration beginning. It's a bit like other risks I've thought about. You don't need to be confident it will happen to think it's worth taking out insurance.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether rapid progress is plausible and its effects on safety and governance, but does not say that the implications depend on the level of AI capability reached by year’s end.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that "five years of progress in one year" is a slogan that sounds precise but actually bundles together several quite different claims, and they don't stand or fall together.

The strongest version is something like: once AI systems can do the work of AI researchers, you get a feedback loop where the systems improve themselves, and so the pace of algorithmic progress accelerates dramatically, maybe by a factor of five or more. I take that scenario seriously. It's not science fiction. But when I actually try to work through it, I find myself more sceptical than many people in this space about how much of the acceleration survives contact with the real world.

The reason is that progress in AI has never been purely a matter of ideas. If you look at what's actually driven the last decade, a very large share of it has been compute and data, not clever algorithms. And compute is physical. You need fabs, you need power, you need datacentres, you need cooling. Those things have lead times measured in years, and they're constrained by capital, by supply chains, by permitting, by electricity grids. An automated researcher can think a hundred times faster than a human, but it can't make TSMC build a fab a hundred times faster. So even if you compress the cognitive labour, you've only compressed one of the inputs.

Then there's the question of experiments. A lot of research is bottlenecked not on thinking but on running things and waiting for results. If your key experiments take weeks of training time on your biggest cluster, then no matter how many brilliant hypotheses your AI researchers generate, you can only test a handful of them per month. You might get better at choosing which experiments to run, and that's genuinely valuable, but it's a much smaller multiplier than five.

So my honest assessment is something like this. I'd put meaningful probability on a significant speed-up in the algorithmic side of progress once AI R&D is substantially automated, perhaps a doubling or tripling of the rate at which ideas get generated and refined. But when you fold in the physical constraints, I'd expect the overall rate of capability progress to accelerate more modestly than the headline number suggests, at least in the first few years. The full "five years in one" picture requires that algorithmic progress can substitute for compute to a degree we haven't really seen demonstrated.

The thing I'd add is that even a two-fold acceleration would be an extraordinary event by historical standards. We've organised our institutions, our regulation, our ability to notice problems and respond to them, around a certain tempo of change. Halving the time we have to react is already enough to make me very worried about whether we can keep up. So I'd caution against treating the question as "is it five or is it one and a half?" and then relaxing if the answer comes in low. The policy-relevant point is that we're plausibly entering a period where the pace outruns our capacity to govern it, and that holds across most of the range I consider likely.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses possible acceleration and its constraints, but does not say that the implications depend on the level of AI capability reached by year’s end.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a possibility worth taking seriously, but I’d want to be quite careful about what we mean by “five years of progress.” We don’t have a simple unit of AI progress, and the pace has already been changing. So this is really a claim about how much faster things could move than we currently expect.

The mechanism that makes it plausible is AI contributing to AI research. If systems can help researchers write code, design experiments, and interpret results, then improvements in AI could accelerate the process that produces further improvements. But that doesn’t establish that we’ll get a fivefold speedup. There could be bottlenecks in compute, in running experiments, or in knowing which research directions are actually promising.

What concerns me is the possibility that technical progress accelerates much more than our ability to respond. Work that we thought we had several years to do—on safety, on evaluating systems, on governance—might have to happen within a year. So I wouldn’t treat that degree of compression as a confident forecast. I would treat it as a serious possibility that our preparations need to accommodate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about the speed and consequences of accelerated progress, but does not state that the implications depend on the AI capability reached by the end of the year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I’d want to be careful about what we mean by five years of progress. There isn’t a fixed quantity of progress that happens each year, so this is really a claim about how sharply the pace might accelerate.

One reason to take it seriously is that AI could start contributing substantially to AI research itself. You could then have a feedback loop: better systems help you build better systems, which help you build still better ones. That doesn’t establish that the process will be extremely fast. Experiments take time, chips take time to manufacture, and some research problems may remain difficult even with a great deal of assistance.

But from the perspective of managing the risks, I think the possibility matters enormously. Five years of technical change in one year wouldn’t automatically give us five years of safety research, institutional learning, or international coordination. Those things have their own bottlenecks. So I wouldn’t confidently predict that degree of acceleration, but I would want our preparations to be robust to it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the pace of acceleration and its risks, but does not state that the implications depend on the AI capability reached by year’s end.
